extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of poetics, literary critics, translators of classical texts
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and evaluative criteria drawn from Aristotle's Poetics (with editorial glosses) for composing and judging poetry—especially epic and tragedy—including meter, unity, plausibility, diction, characterization, and appropriate use of spectacle versus narration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate magnitude / sufficient length
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a 'terminus sufficiens longitudinis' — a sufficient limit of length: the work must have a beginning and an end in which there is power; different genres have different appropriate lengths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epic (Iliad, Odyssey) is long and can be composed of many parts; tragedy is briefer and generally treats a single session/action. Choose the scope so the beginning and ending have authority and the piece sustains its chosen kind (ancients' compositions were often shorter; tragedies tend to be shorter than epics).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genre-appropriate meter
rubrics_metrics.description: The heroic meter (hexameter) is fitted by experience to the epic; different meters suit different functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The heroic (epic) meter is grand, receives glosses and additions, and allows elaborate language and metaphors. Iambic and tetrameter are kinetic—associated with acting, chorus, and practical movement. It is improper to construct a long system in a meter other than that of the poem; mixing meters awkwardly (as Chaeremon did) is shameful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity and constitution of action (single action for tragedy)
rubrics_metrics.description: The constitution and length of parts differ by genre; the fitting limit is where the work has beginning and end and power; tragedies typically have one continuous action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For tragedy, keep to a single action/session (unity of action). Epics can comprise many episodes and parts; ensure each part is fittingly divided according to the nature of the work so the whole attains its end.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate use of spectacle vs narration (showing vs telling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Tragedy cannot easily imitate many parts when enacted (what actors show on stage) while epic can narrate at length; what can be imitated on stage differs from what can be narrated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide what to present directly (on stage, by actors) and what to narrate. Epic may accomplish vast narration and thus accumulate 'ogkos' (bulk/magnitude); tragedy must select what is representable. Use narrative where imitation on stage would be impractical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy and concision of diction/character-introduction
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet should speak little in introducing a person; Homerness: Homer 'knows what to do' and introduces a man, woman, or custom with few words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer brief prooemions/intros that immediately introduce a character in their customary behavior rather than long contests of description. Excessive explanation or over-elaboration in introductions is less artful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of the marvelous / produce wonder (to astonish appropriately)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is fitting in tragedy to make the marvelous (tau thauma) occur; the marvelous affects the hearer and can be used to change or move the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tragedy should contain incidents that provoke wonder (but not ridiculousness). Epic may produce wonder through narrative and analogies; ensure the marvelous is used to enhance the work, not to create satiety (too-similar episodes quickly weary the audience).

rubrics_metrics.name: Plausibility, probability, and permissible falsehood (eikos vs pseudos)
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet is an imitator and must observe what is plausible (eikos); outright falsehoods (pseudos) are generally faults, but can be justified if they serve other goods (as Homer sometimes does). Prefer the probable-impossible to the possible-improbable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid contradictions and the preposterous; if the first element of the story is false, subsequent additions must be necessarily consistent. Some falsehoods may be permitted when they secure greater poetic goods (e.g., Homeric departures that enhance the admirable). When judging, consider whether something is impossible, improbable, or acceptable by poetic convention.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance of the absurd/preposterous (atomos/atopon) and of purely irrational elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not include what is preposterous (involving contradiction or violation of natural order) or irrational in a way that betrays artistic weakness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Elements that are obviously unnecessary or impossible should not be made part of the poem; if an oddity appears, it must be defensible by the art or by other values in the poem. Distinguish between what is improbable but acceptable and what is preposterous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of faults: intrinsic vs accidental
rubrics_metrics.description: Poetic fault is twofold: that which is in the craft itself (intrinsic) and that which is accidental (circumstantial).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When criticising, determine whether a fault arises from the nature of the art (a genuine artistic mistake) or from accidental ignorance or manner. Criticisms should be examined with respect to the end of the art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Five categories of indictments against a poem
rubrics_metrics.description: Accusations brought against poets fall into five kinds: that the poem is impossible, irrational (alogon), harmful to the art, contrary, or nonconforming to the correctness required by the craft.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When responding to critique, address which of the five charges is being made and consult the appropriate remedies; Aristotle lists how to examine each type and to supply solutions (twelve types of solutions are enumerated elsewhere).

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of reproofs and their grounds (five-fold charge leading to twelve solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reproofs (epitimemata) may be that something is impossible, irrational, damaging to the art, contrary, or outside the craft's correctness; solutions (lyseis) to such reproofs are multiple (twelve enumerated).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critics should classify complaints and consult recognized lines of reply (e.g., show that something is not impossible, is plausible, serves the art, or corresponds to customary usage).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriateness of diction: avoid too bright or inappropriate phraseology
rubrics_metrics.description: Diction should not be excessively brilliant (liān lamprà) in argo passages, for bright expression can conceal or mask character and thought.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider the effect of words, metaphors, and prosody; choose language suited to the parts (ethical, intellectual, or mere ornament), and attend to prosodic devices, metaphors, idioms and translation issues (names and transferred meanings require scrutiny).

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitative object-choice: depict what is/was/seems/ought to be
rubrics_metrics.description: The poet imitates from among three kinds of things: what was or is, what seems to be, and what ought to be; one must determine which of these is being represented.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decide whether the poem purports to depict reality, appearance, or an ethical/ideal model; this affects diction, characterization, and plausibility standards. As with painters, select the aspect to imitate consistently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character-evidence: present characters with coherent ethos (êthos)
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters introduced should have evident and consistent 'êthos' (dispositions); the poet can introduce a man, woman, or other character with little but must preserve plausibility of ethos.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Introduce characters in ways that make their moral character recognizable and not unnatural; avoid introducing bizarre or 'unfitting' behavior without cause. Evaluate whether a dramatized person has actions consistent with the presented ethos.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider audience capacity and differing effects for good vs poor spectators
rubrics_metrics.description: Different genres and practices have different audiences: e.g., epic is fit for 'better' spectators, with more discursive narration; some spectacle and movement appeal to lesser spectators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When composing, account for the intended spectators. Some arts (epic) suppose reflective reception; tragedy and spectacle rely on visible movement and can influence different audiences. The poet should calibrate complexity and spectacle according to the audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid sameness and repetition (prevent satiety)
rubrics_metrics.description: Rapid recurrence of similar elements causes satiety (simile satietatem affert cito) and makes parts fall away from effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Vary episodes and avoid quickly filling the work with too-similar incidents. Similarity, if excessive, undermines tragedy's effect and the hearer's engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate handling of transferred/figurative names and expressions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a name or phrase seems to mean something contrary (e.g., a name appearing opposite to its usual sense), check how much it signifies in context and whether the transfer is justifiable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigate the semantic range of words and names (translations, local usages). Ensure metaphors and transferred meanings suit the passage's function and are intelligible to the audience/readers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose imitation extent consistent with the art's end
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge faults with regard to the art's end; what is tolerable for making the work more striking toward its end may be permitted if it achieves the poetic purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing an element as a defect, consider whether it detracts from or serves the poem's intended end (glory, effect, moral purpose). Some devices that depart from literal truth may be defensible if they elevate the poem's artistic result.
